g.title: Pronouns
g.rule:
English has several sets of pronouns. Choose by the job the word does in the sentence.

subject · objectShe called me. · They named him after his uncle.
possessive adjective · possessive pronounIt's my name. · The idea was mine.
reflexiveI introduced myself. · She taught herself.
two objectsThey gave her a nickname. · They gave it to her.

ex.q: My parents named ___ after my grandmother.
Is this pen yours or ___?
He introduced ___ to the class.

talk: How did your parents choose your name? Do you like it?
Which names are popular in your country now, and which sound old-fashioned?

r.text:
My first name is Aleksandra, but almost nobody uses it. At home they call me Sasha, which is short for Aleksandra, and my friends gave me the nickname "Echo" at school because I repeated everything the teacher said.

I was named after my grandmother. She thought the name was old-fashioned and never liked it herself, so she was surprised when my parents chose it for me.

My surname is harder. Foreign colleagues can't pronounce it, and I have to spell it every time I book a hotel. When I got married, I decided not to change my name. My husband kept his, and I kept mine. On official forms I still write my maiden name, and I sign emails with my initials, A.K.

People sometimes ask which name is really me. The answer is simple: all of them are mine. I just introduce myself differently to different people.

ex.q: Why was the writer called "Echo" at school?
o: She repeated what the teacher said

ex.q: Her grandmother loved the name Aleksandra.
What did she do when she got married?
How does she sign emails?

l.intro: A couple are choosing a name for their baby daughter.

script.t: Arman, we have to choose a first name this week. The hospital asked me again.
I know. My mother wants us to name her after my grandmother, Zeynep.
It's a lovely name, but people here can't pronounce it. She'll have to spell it all her life.
That's true. What about Amina? It's short and nobody gets it wrong.
I like it. But there are three Aminas in my office.
Then something old-fashioned. Roza? Those names are coming back.
Roza. Hmm. Her friends would call her Rosie. I don't mind that nickname.
And with our surname, her initials would be R.A. That looks fine.
Let's give her both. Roza Zeynep. Your mother will be happy, and so will I.
Perfect. I'll tell her myself tonight.

ex.q: Who wants the baby to be called Zeynep?
Madina thinks Zeynep is easy to pronounce.
What is the problem with the name Amina?
o: It is very common in Madina's office

ex.q: What do they decide?

g.title: Adjectives
g.rule:
Three things to know about adjectives.

comparingBlue is more calming than red. · It's the brightest room in the house.
the + adjective = a groupThe young prefer bright colours.
one / onesI like the blue shirt, but I prefer the green one.

ex.q: This is ___ colour in the shop.

talk: What is your favourite colour, and what does it make you feel?
Describe the colours of your home. Would you change any?

r.text:
When Ruslan opened his first café, he painted the walls bright red. "I wanted something powerful," he says. "Red was the most fashionable colour that year." The café was full, but customers left quickly, and the staff found long shifts stressful.

A designer friend suggested a change. Pale green and neutral cream are more calming than red, she explained, and people stay longer in rooms that feel relaxed. Ruslan was not convinced. He thought the new colours looked dull. In the end he agreed to paint one wall, the biggest one.

The result surprised him. Customers stayed longer and ordered more. The young still chose the colourful tables near the window, while older customers preferred the quieter ones at the back.

Ruslan has now repainted every wall. "It was the most affordable change I have ever made," he says, "and the most useful." He kept one cheerful red door.

ex.q: Why did Ruslan first choose red?
At first Ruslan liked the idea of pale colours.
What happened after he painted one wall?
What is still red?

l.intro: Two flatmates are in a paint shop.

script.t: Yerlan, look at this yellow. It's so cheerful.
It's very bright. I think it would be more stressful than cheerful after a week.
You always choose the dullest colour in the shop.
Not the dullest. Something neutral, like this pale grey one.
Grey? Our living room is the darkest room in the flat. It needs colour.
OK, that's a fair point. What about a pale green? It's more calming than yellow.
Let me see. Yes, that one is nice. Is it affordable?
It's cheaper than the yellow one, actually. And it's suitable for kitchens too.
Good. Then green walls, and I'll buy some colourful cushions.
Deal. But I'm choosing the curtains.

ex.q: What does Kamila like at first?
Their living room gets a lot of light.
Why does Yerlan suggest pale green?
What will Kamila buy?

lessons.title: Reading: The colour of a room

g.title: Present tenses
g.rule:
Choose between the present simple and the present continuous.

ex.q: We ___ to Istanbul on Saturday. I've got the tickets.

talk: How do you prepare for a trip? What do you always pack?
Are you travelling anywhere in the next few months? What are your plans?

r.text:
My sister and I are flying to Istanbul on Friday. The flight leaves at seven in the morning, so we are setting off from home at four. We are the same age and we come from the same family, but we pack in completely different ways.

Dinara starts a week before. She writes a list, then she lays everything on the bed: passport, charger, adaptor, toiletries, a small first-aid kit and a guidebook. She always travels with hand luggage only. "A big suitcase makes you slow," she says.

I usually pack at the last minute. As I write this, it is Thursday evening and I am still looking for my backpack. I never make a list, and I nearly always forget something. Last year it was my charger. The year before, it was my passport, and we almost missed the plane.

This time Dinara is checking my bag before we leave.

ex.q: What time does the flight leave?
Dinara usually takes a big suitcase.
What is the writer doing on Thursday evening?
What did the writer forget the year before last?

l.intro: A brother phones his sister the evening before their trip.

script.t: Aliya, are you ready? The taxi is coming at five tomorrow morning.
Almost. I'm packing my suitcase right now.
Now? You always do everything at the last minute.
I work better that way. Do I need an adaptor?
Yes, the plugs are different there. I'm taking two, so you can have one.
Thanks. And I can't find my charger. I usually keep it by the bed.
Check your backpack. You left it there last time.
You're right, here it is. What about the guidebook?
It's in my hand luggage, with the passports and the first-aid kit.
You have my passport? Good. Then I only need to pack my toiletries.
Please set an alarm. We're setting off at five, not at ten past.

ex.q: What time is the taxi coming?
Aliya packed her suitcase a week ago.
Where was Aliya's charger?
Who has the passports?

lessons.title: Listening: The night before the flight

talk: Which local shops do you use, and which things do you buy online?
Describe your best or worst experience of shopping online.

r.text:
Twenty years ago, Mill Street had a baker's, a chemist's, a dry cleaner's and three clothes shops. Today only the baker's and the hairdresser's are still open. The estate agent's on the corner closed in the spring.

"People fill a basket online and go to checkout without leaving the sofa," says Marta, the baker's daughter, who now runs the family shop. "Delivery is free, there is always a discount, and if something is wrong, you get a refund in two days."

So why do her customers still come? Marta thinks the answer is service. She knows her customers' names and their children's names. If a loaf is not in stock, she keeps one for you the next day. Nobody asks for a receipt.

A friend of hers has just opened a small bookshop next door. "The street isn't dead," Marta says. "It is just changing."

ex.q: Which shops are still open on Mill Street?
o: The chemist's and the dry cleaner's

ex.q: Marta's mother or father had the shop before her.
Why does Marta think customers still come?
What has opened next door?

l.intro: A customer returns a jacket to a shop.

script.t: Good morning. I bought this jacket last week, and I'd like a refund, please.
Of course. Is there a problem with it?
It's my husband's size, but the sleeves are too long.
I see. Do you have the receipt?
Yes, here it is. I paid by card at the checkout.
Thank you. We could change it for a smaller one. Let me check if it's in stock.
That would be even better, actually.
I'm afraid we don't have it here. But our other shop, the one next to the chemist's, has two.
That's at the other end of town. Is delivery possible?
Yes, to your home in two days, and it's free. I'll also give you a ten per cent discount on your next visit.
Wonderful. A friend of mine told me the service here was good.

ex.q: What is wrong with the jacket?
The customer has lost her receipt.
Where is the smaller jacket?
What does the assistant offer?
o: A refund and a new jacket

lessons.title: Reading: The last shops on Mill Street

g.title: Past simple, past continuous, or used to?
g.rule:
Three ways to talk about the past.

a finished action → past simpleI left school in 2015.
an action in progress → past continuousI was living with my parents when I met her.
a past habit or state → used toI used to play outside every day. · We didn't use to have a car.

ex.q: When I was a child, we ___ every summer at my grandmother's.
I ___ home when I saw the accident.
Did you ___ (use to) wear a uniform?

talk: What did you use to do as a child that you don't do now?
Were your parents strict? What were you allowed to do?

r.text:
My grandfather is retired now, and he loves telling stories about his childhood. He grew up in a small village in the 1960s. "We used to leave the house after breakfast and come back when it was dark," he says. "Nobody knew where we were."

His parents were strict about some things. He was not allowed to speak at the table, and he had to be polite to every adult in the village. But he was free in ways that surprise me. He was driving a tractor when he was twelve.

My parents brought me up very differently. When I was a teenager, I had to phone home every two hours. I didn't use to go anywhere alone until I was fifteen.

Now I am in my twenties, and my own daughter is a toddler. I often wonder which kind of parent I am going to be. My grandfather laughs. "A worried one," he says. "We all were."

ex.q: Where did the grandfather grow up?
He was allowed to talk during meals.
What did the writer have to do as a teenager?
How old is the writer now?

l.intro: A teenager asks her grandfather about his childhood.

script.t: Grandad, were your parents strict?
Very. I wasn't allowed to stay out after eight, even when I was sixteen.
Eight! What did you use to do in the evenings?
We used to read, or listen to the radio. We didn't use to have a television.
That sounds boring.
It wasn't. I was reading an adventure book when I first decided to become a sailor.
And did you?
I did. I left home at eighteen and worked on ships until I was middle-aged.
Did you bring Mum up the same way? Was she allowed to go out?
More than I was. Your grandmother was the strict one. I was usually at sea.
So that's why Mum says she grew up with two captains.

ex.q: What time did Grandad have to be home?
His family had a television.
What was he doing when he decided to become a sailor?
Who was the strict parent for Tomiris's mother?

lessons.title: Past simple, past continuous, or used to?

Listening: When I was your age

g.title: Prepositions
g.rule:

movementwalk along the beach · go through the gate · jump into the water

talk: Describe a favourite photo: who is in it, and where are they?
Do you print your photos or leave them on your phone? Why?

r.text:
There are hundreds of pictures in my mother's albums, but one is my favourite. Somebody took it at my grandparents' house in the summer of 1994.

In the foreground, my mother is sitting on the grass. She is about twenty and she is laughing at something. On the left, my grandfather is standing next to his old car. He is very proud of it. In the middle, there is a table with a watermelon on it, and behind the table you can see the apple trees. In the background, a small boy is running through the gate. That is my uncle.

It is not a good photo. It is a little out of focus, and somebody's finger is in the corner. But when I zoom in on the faces, everybody looks happy.

Last month I had it printed and put it on my wall. A perfect portrait would not mean as much.

ex.q: Who is in the foreground of the photo?

What is wrong with the photo?

l.intro: Two friends look at an old school photo.

script.t: Laura, look what I found in my mother's album. Our class, twenty years ago.
No! Let me see. Where am I?
You're in the middle, next to the teacher. You're holding a cat.
A cat? Oh yes, it lived at the school. And who's that on the left?
That's me. I'm the one with the terrible haircut.
And the tall boy behind you?
That's Ruslan. He's a doctor now. Can you see the girl in the foreground, sitting on the floor?
It's a bit out of focus. Zoom in. Is that Saule?
Yes. And in the background, through the window, you can see the old sports hall.
They knocked it down years ago. Dias, can you print this for me?
I'll print two. One for you and one for Saule.

g.title: Future forms: will / shall and be going to
g.rule:
Choose the form by the kind of future.

a plan → be going toI'm going to recycle more this year.
a decision now, an offer, a promise → willThe bin is full. I'll empty it.
a suggestion or offer → shallShall I take the rubbish out? · Shall we repair it?
a predictionPrices will rise. · Look, it's going to fall.

ex.q: ___ I help you carry those bags?

Don't worry, I ___ (not / throw) it away.

talk: What are you going to do to waste less this year?
Do you think people will recycle more in the future? Why or why not?

r.text:
Last month our family tried an experiment. We decided that we were going to throw away as little as possible for thirty days.

The first week was hard. Almost everything we bought came in plastic packaging, and the kitchen bin was full by Wednesday. "This won't work," said my son. "I'll take the rubbish out."

Then we changed our habits. We took our own bags to the market, and we started to reuse glass jars. Leftovers became lunch for the next day. My daughter bought a second-hand jacket and discovered that she liked it more than a new one.

We still made some waste, but by the end of the month we were filling one small bag a week. Before, it was five.

Are we going to continue? Yes, though not perfectly. Our city does not recycle everything, and a lot still goes to landfill. But if every family did the same, the environment would feel the difference.

ex.q: How long did the experiment last?
The first week was easy.
What did the daughter buy?
How much rubbish did they make at the end?

l.intro: Two flatmates talk about the rubbish.

script.t: Timur, the bin is full again. And it smells.
Sorry. I'll take the rubbish out in a minute.
You said that yesterday. And look, you threw away three glass jars.
Were they useful?
We can reuse them. I'm going to keep rice and pasta in them.
OK. Shall I wash them?
Yes, please. And from now on I'm going to put a second bin here, just for packaging.
Does our building recycle?
It does. There are new containers outside. Most people don't use them, so everything goes to landfill.
I didn't know. I'll start today. And shall we eat the leftovers from last night?
Good idea. Less waste, and no cooking.

ex.q: What is the problem at the start?
Timur took the rubbish out yesterday.
What is Asel going to do with the jars?
What will they have for dinner?

lessons.title: Future forms: will / shall and be going to

talk: What would you study if you could start again?
What will you do if you get the chance to work abroad?

r.text:
Timur and his twin sister Aigerim finished school with the same marks, and then chose opposite directions.

Aigerim went to university. She is going to graduate next summer with a degree in economics. She has done one internship at a bank, and she has a part-time job in a café at weekends. "If I had more experience, I would feel more confident," she says. "My qualification is good, but everybody has one."

Timur did not apply for university. He started an apprenticeship with an engineering company instead. He attends college one day a week, and the company pays him. "If I work hard, they will offer me a permanent job in the spring," he says. He already has practical skills that his sister does not have.

Who made the better choice? Their mother refuses to answer. "If I were eighteen again," she says, "I would probably do both."

ex.q: What is Aigerim studying?

How often does Timur attend college?

l.intro: A student asks a career adviser for help.

script.t: I want to apply for a job at a design company, but the deadline is on Friday.
That's enough time. Tell me about your experience.
Not much. I have a part-time job in a shop, and I did a two-week internship last summer.
That's a start. And your qualifications?
I'm going to graduate in June. My degree is in graphic design.
Good. If I were you, I would put the internship at the top of your CV.
Even if it was only two weeks?
Yes. If you describe the skills you learned, they'll see what you can do.
And if they ask about a permanent job? I'm still a student.
Be honest. If you tell them you graduate in June, they won't be surprised later.
Thank you. I'll send it tonight, unless my internet stops again.

ex.q: When is the deadline?
Alibek has a lot of work experience.
What should Alibek put at the top of his CV?
What does the adviser tell him to be?

r.text:
I have just done something I am not proud of. I have watched a complete season of a detective series in one weekend. Ten episodes, nine hours.

I am not the only one. My colleague has already seen every documentary on her favourite channel, and my brother has never watched the news on a television. He streams everything on his phone, usually with subtitles because he watches on the bus.

When I was a child, things were different. Our family watched one episode a week, and we argued about the remote control. If you missed a programme, you missed it.

Is binge-watching bad for us? I have read several articles this month, and they don't agree. What I have noticed is this: I can't remember the plot of the series I watched last weekend. But I still remember the reality show my family laughed at twenty years ago, including the name of the presenter.

ex.q: What has the writer just done?
o: Watched ten episodes in a weekend

ex.q: The writer's brother watches the news on television.
Why does the brother use subtitles?
What does the writer still remember?

l.intro: Two colleagues talk about a series at lunch.

script.t: Oleg, have you seen the new detective series yet?
I've just started it. I've watched two episodes.
Only two? I've already finished the whole season.
When? It came out on Friday!
I binge-watched it at the weekend. I haven't slept much.
Don't tell me who did it. I've never guessed the ending of a series, and I want to try.
I won't. Have you noticed the presenter from the evening news? He plays the judge.
No! I watch it in the original with subtitles, so I didn't recognise his voice.
It's on the same channel as that cooking reality show, by the way.
I haven't watched ordinary TV this year. I stream everything.
Then finish it tonight. I can't keep the secret until tomorrow.

ex.q: How many episodes has Oleg watched?
Dana watched the series slowly over a month.
Who plays the judge?
How does Oleg watch television?

lessons.title: Reading: Have you finished it yet?

talk: Would you rather live in the country or in a city? Why?

r.text:
We have been living in the valley for two years now. Before that, we had a flat in the city, and I had been complaining about the noise for a long time.

Our house is at the end of a path, next to a field. There is a stream at the bottom of the garden and a hedge full of birds. Our nearest neighbour is a farmer who keeps cattle. We have known him since our first week, when he pulled our car out of the mud.

Is it peaceful? Yes. Is it perfect? No. My husband has been commuting to the city every day, and it takes him ninety minutes each way. In winter we sometimes feel isolated, and the internet stops when the wind is strong.

Recently I have been repairing the old barn. My hands are tired and my back hurts, but I have been sleeping better than ever. I don't think we will go back.

ex.q: How long has the family lived in the valley?
They met their neighbour when he helped them with their car.
What is one problem with life there?

l.intro: A woman visits an old friend who moved to the countryside.

script.t: Pavel, it's so peaceful here. How long have you been living on the farm?
Since last spring. So about a year and a half.
And you look tired. What have you been doing?
I've been repairing the barn roof all morning. And the cattle got into the neighbour's field again.
Do you miss the city?
Sometimes. It's a bit isolated in winter. The path to the road disappears under the snow.
And work? Have you been commuting?
No, I've been working from home. The internet is slow, but it's enough.
I've been thinking about leaving the city too. I've known for years that I'm not happy there.
Come and stay for a month first. Walk along the stream, feed the animals, and then decide.
A month without traffic. I'll bring my boots.

g.rule:
Choose the verb by how strong the rule or advice is.

talk: What are the rules of good manners in a restaurant in your country?
Describe the best or worst service you have had in a restaurant.

r.text:
I have been a waiter for eleven years, and I would like to share a few rules.

First, you should book a table at the weekend. You don't have to book on a Tuesday, but on Saturday we are full by seven.

Second, you needn't order a starter, a main course and a dessert. Nobody is counting. But you must tell us about allergies before you order, not after we serve the food.

Third, if you ask for your steak rare, it will be rare. You shouldn't send it back because it is pink.

Fourth, please complain. If something is wrong, you ought to tell us immediately, when we can still fix it. You mustn't wait until you get home and then write an angry review.

Finally, the bill. In our restaurant there is a service charge, so you don't have to leave a tip. If you do, thank you. I will remember your face, and your table by the window.

ex.q: When should you book a table?
You have to order three courses.
When must you tell the waiter about allergies?
Why is a tip not necessary in this restaurant?

l.intro: A guest orders dinner for herself and her husband.

script.t: Good evening. Are you ready to order?
Almost. Do we have to order a starter, or can we just have a main course?
You don't have to, madam. But you should try the soup. It's the chef's favourite.
Then one soup to share, please. And I'll have the steak.
How would you like it?
Rare, please. And my husband would like the fish, but he mustn't eat nuts.
I'll tell the kitchen. There are no nuts in the fish, but you ought to avoid the chocolate cake on the dessert menu.
Thank you. Do we need to pay a service charge?
It's included in the bill, so you needn't leave a tip.
That's good to know. Oh, and one more thing. We booked a table by the window.
I'm so sorry. Give me two minutes and I'll move you.

ex.q: What do the guests order to start?
The woman wants her steak well cooked.
What can't her husband eat?

g.title: can, could and be able to
g.rule:

ex.q: I've never ___ put up a shelf.
The door was stuck, but I ___ open it in the end.

talk: Which repairs can you do yourself, and which do you pay for?
Describe an object when you don't know its name: It's a kind of…

r.text:
I have never been able to fix things. My father could repair anything, but I could not even change a light bulb without reading the instructions.

Last month I decided to put up a shelf by myself. How hard could it be? I bought a drill, a screwdriver and a box of screws. I already had a hammer and some nails, so I felt ready.

On the first weekend I made four holes in the wrong place. On the second, I managed to put up the shelf, but it was not straight, and my books slid to one end. I also fell off the ladder, though not far.

On the third weekend a neighbour lent me a tool I had never seen before. It's a kind of ruler with a bubble in it, and it shows you when something is flat.

The shelf is straight now. I would like to be able to say I enjoyed it. Next, I am going to fix the kitchen tap.

ex.q: What could the writer's father do?
The shelf was straight on the second weekend.
What did the neighbour lend the writer?
o: A tool that shows if something is flat

ex.q: What is the writer's next job?

l.intro: A woman phones her brother about a problem in her kitchen.

script.t: Nurlan, the kitchen tap is dripping again. Can you come and fix it?
I can't today. I'll be able to come on Saturday.
Saturday? I haven't been able to sleep because of the noise.
Then do it yourself. I could change a tap when I was fourteen.
I've never used a tool in my life. I can't even put up a picture.
It's easy. Do you have a screwdriver?
I have a hammer, some nails and a paintbrush.
Not helpful. Ask your neighbour for a tool. It's a kind of metal key that opens wide.
And then?
Turn off the water first. That's the important part. Then call me, and I'll explain every step.
All right. If I manage to do it, you're buying me dinner.

ex.q: When can Nurlan come?
Aigul often repairs things at home.
What does Aigul have at home?

g.title: Phrasal verbs
g.rule:
A phrasal verb is a verb + a small word. Word order depends on the type.

no objectThe machine broke down.
separable: noun in two placesTake out the money. · Take the money out.

ex.q: I borrowed ten dollars. I'll ___ tomorrow.
Could you ___ my bag for a minute?

talk: Do you prefer paying by cash, card or phone? Why?
Tell the story of a time you lost or forgot your card.

r.text:
My bank card stopped working on a Monday, and I found out how much I depend on it.

I had run out of cash the day before. I went to a cash machine to take some out, typed my PIN, and the machine kept the card. No money, no card, and a balance I could not check.

The bank promised to send a new one in five days. Until then I could not withdraw anything, and of course I could not use contactless payment on the bus. A colleague lent me some money. "Pay me back when you can," she said. I wrote the amount down so that I would give it back exactly.

It was a strange week. I walked to work. I took my lunch from home. I looked after every coin.

When the card finally arrived, I paid my colleague back and paid in the rest of my coins. I had spent a third of what I usually spend.

ex.q: What happened at the cash machine?
The bank sent a new card the next day.
Who helped the writer?
What did the writer learn?
o: He or she usually spends much more

l.intro: Two friends are outside a cinema.

script.t: Irina, I've run out of cash. Could you pay for my ticket? I'll pay you back tomorrow.
Why don't you pay by card? They take contactless.
I left my card at home. I took it out of my wallet this morning and forgot to put it back.
There's a cash machine over there.
Without a card? And I can never remember my PIN anyway.
Bekzat, you still owe me for the pizza last week.
I know. I wrote it down. I'll give it all back on Friday when my salary comes in.
OK. But this time I'm sending you a message so you can't forget.
Fair. I found out yesterday that my balance is almost zero, so thank you.
Then no popcorn for you.
I'll look after your coat. That's worth some popcorn.

ex.q: Why can't Bekzat pay?
o: He has no cash or card with him

ex.q: Bekzat already owes Irina money.
When will he pay her back?

g.title: Verb patterns
g.rule:
The first verb decides the form of the second.

+ -ingenjoy, fancy, feel like, mind, recommend: I enjoy going to gigs.
+ todecide, manage, want, need, would like: We decided to stay in.

talk: Do you prefer going out or staying in? What do you enjoy doing?
Describe the best live performance you have seen.

r.text:
Every Friday, Zarina and her husband Daniyar have the same conversation.

Daniyar enjoys going out. He fancies seeing a live gig at a small venue, standing near the stage with a noisy audience. Last month he persuaded Zarina to go to a concert that was almost sold out, and they stood for three hours. "He made me stay until the end," she says.

Zarina would rather stay in. If they go out at all, she wants to see a play, with a comfortable seat in the fifth row and an ice cream in the interval. She doesn't mind paying more for that.

They have decided to take turns. This week it was her choice, so Daniyar agreed to go to the theatre. He phoned the box office and managed to get the last two tickets.

To his surprise, he loved the performance. "I didn't expect to enjoy it," he says. "Don't tell her. She will want to choose every week."

ex.q: What does Daniyar like doing on Fridays?
Zarina enjoyed standing for three hours.
Where does Zarina like to sit at the theatre?
What did Daniyar think of the play?

l.intro: A man phones a theatre box office.

script.t: Hello, I'd like to book two tickets for the play on Saturday evening.
I'm afraid Saturday evening is sold out. Would you like to come in the afternoon?
My wife wants to see it in the evening. Is there anything on Friday?
Let me check. Yes, I have two seats in row three, near the stage.
Aren't they too close?
Some people enjoy sitting there. But I'd recommend choosing row ten. You can see the whole stage.
Row ten, then. What time does the performance start?
At seven thirty. There's a twenty-minute interval at about half past eight.
Do you let people bring drinks into the theatre?
Only water. We ask the audience to finish other drinks in the café.
Fine. I've managed to surprise her at last. Thank you.

ex.q: Why can't he book Saturday evening?
He books seats in row three.

talk: What do you do to look after yourself?

r.text:
My aunt Gulnara has worked six days a week for thirty years. She cuts her own hair, she paints her own nails, and she has never had a massage in her life. "Why pay somebody?" she always says.

For her sixtieth birthday, my cousins and I decided to change that. We made an appointment at a spa and told her it was a family lunch.

She was not pleased at first. Then she had her hair trimmed and dyed, and she had a manicure. After that she had a facial, which she described as "sleeping with cream on".

In the afternoon she finally agreed to the massage. She fell asleep after five minutes.

Since then, something has changed. She has her hair cut every six weeks now. Last week she had her eyes tested and ordered new glasses, and she is thinking of joining a gym.

"You should treat yourself sometimes," she told me yesterday, as if it was her own idea.

ex.q: What did Gulnara always say?

What happened during the massage?
What did she do last week?

l.intro: A woman phones a salon before a family wedding.

script.t: Hello, I'd like to make an appointment for Friday, please. For two people.
Certainly. What would you like to have done?
I'm going to have my hair cut and dyed. My sister only wants a trim.
We can do both at ten. Would you like a manicure as well?
Yes, I'd like to have my nails done. How long does it take?
About forty minutes. We also have a special offer on a facial or a massage this week.
I've never had a massage. Is it expensive?
It's half price until Sunday. Many people have one after their haircut.
Then I'll treat myself. One massage for me, and a facial for my sister.
Lovely. So Friday at ten, hair for two, one manicure, one massage and one facial.
Perfect. We'll look wonderful, and we won't have done anything ourselves.

g.title: The passive; defining and non-defining relative clauses
g.rule:
Two tools for describing places and their history.

ex.q: The cathedral ___ in the fifteenth century.
The castle, ___ is on a hill, has three towers.

talk: Describe a historic building in your country: when was it built, and by whom?
Which historic place would you most like to visit? Why?

r.text:
This text describes an invented place. It shows how guidebooks describe historic sites.

The castle of Karatas, which stands on a hill above the river, was built in the twelfth century. For two hundred years it protected the town that grew around its walls.

In 1340 the region was invaded from the north. The battle lasted three days, the local army was defeated, and most of the castle was destroyed. Only the main tower, which is forty metres high, was left standing.

The ruins were forgotten for centuries. Farmers used the stones to build their houses, and trees grew inside the old walls.

The site has been restored over the last thirty years by a team whose work is paid for by visitors. The tower can now be climbed, and a small monument has been put up in the place where the gate once stood.

The palace and cathedral in the town below, which are much younger, are also open to the public.

ex.q: When was the castle built?
The local army won the battle.
What did farmers do with the stones?
Who pays for the restoration?

l.intro: A guide answers a tourist's questions. The city is invented.

script.t: Excuse me, when was this cathedral built?
It was started in the fourteenth century, but it wasn't finished for two hundred years.
Why did it take so long?
The city was invaded twice, and the work was stopped each time.
And the tower, which looks newer?
You have good eyes. The first tower was destroyed in a storm. This one was added about a century ago.
What's the building that we can see on the hill?
That's the old palace, where the governor used to live. It's being restored at the moment.
Can it be visited?
Only the gardens. The rooms will be opened next year. But the monument that stands in the main square is worth seeing.
Thank you. I'll go there now, before the rain.

ex.q: How long did it take to finish the cathedral?
The first tower was destroyed in a battle.
Who used to live in the palace?
Which part of the palace is open now?

lessons.title: The passive; defining and non-defining relative clauses

g.title: Reported speech
g.rule:
When you report what somebody said, the tense usually moves one step back.

statementI have a bad memory. → He said (that) he had a bad memory.
will → would · can → couldI'll remind you. → She said she would remind me.

ex.q: I can't recall his name. → She said she ___ recall his name.
He asked me where ___.

talk: Do you have a good memory? What do you forget most often?
Tell your partner three things people said to you this week.

r.text:
My uncle Bolat is the most forgetful person I know, and his sixtieth birthday proved it.

My aunt had planned a surprise party. She told him that they were going to a restaurant, and she asked him to be home by six. He said that he would remember. She even put a reminder on his phone.

At six, forty guests were waiting in the dark. At seven, my aunt phoned him. He said he was at the garage and asked if something was wrong. She reminded him about the restaurant. He told her that he had completely forgotten and that he couldn't leave because the car was in pieces.

He finally arrived at nine, in dirty clothes. He didn't recognize half the guests in the dark.

The strange thing is that Bolat knows hundreds of poems by heart, and he can recall every football result since 1990. "My memory is fine," he told us. "It just chooses what to remember." It was an unforgettable evening.

ex.q: What did Bolat's wife ask him to do?
Bolat was at the garage at seven o'clock.
Why couldn't he leave immediately?
What can Bolat remember well?

l.intro: A man tells his colleague about a phone call from their boss.

script.t: Samal, the director phoned while you were at lunch.
Oh no. What did she say?
She said that she needed the report by four o'clock.
By four? She told me yesterday that I had until Friday.
She said the client had changed the date. She asked if you could send her the first part now.
I can. Did she ask about the photos?
Yes. She asked where they were. I told her I didn't know.
They're on my desk. Did she say anything else?
She asked me to remind you about the meeting tomorrow. She said you'd forgotten the last one.
I didn't forget it! I have a vivid memory of sitting in that room alone.
Then she was the forgetful one. I won't remind her of that.

ex.q: When does the director need the report?
The client changed the date.
Where are the photos?
What did the director ask Erik to do?

g.title: Third conditional and other uses of the past perfect
g.rule:
Use the past perfect for a time before another past time, and to imagine a different past.

earlier pastWhen we arrived, the ceremony had started.
third conditionalIf it hadn't rained, we would have had the party outside.
with adverbsThey had already left. · I had never seen such a cake. · She had just arrived.

ex.q: If the groom ___ the rings, the wedding would have started on time.
When I got there, the guests ___.
If we had booked earlier, we ___ (get) a better room.

talk: Describe a wedding you have been to. Did anything go wrong?
What would have been different in your life if you had made another choice?

r.text:
Everything went wrong at my sister's wedding, and it was the best one I have ever been to.

The ceremony was planned for a garden. By the time the guests arrived, it had already started to rain, and the chairs were wet. The groom had left the rings at home, so the best man drove back to get them. When he returned, the bride had been waiting for forty minutes.

They said their vows under two umbrellas. One bridesmaid lost a shoe in the mud.

The reception was moved into a small barn. There was no room for the band, so the guests sang. My grandmother, who had never danced in public, danced for an hour.

My sister says she wouldn't change anything. If it hadn't rained, we would have sat at separate tables in a big garden. If the day had been perfect, nobody would have remembered it.

They left for their honeymoon the next morning. The sun was shining, of course.

ex.q: Where was the ceremony planned?
The groom remembered to bring the rings.
Why did the guests sing?
o: There was no room for the band

ex.q: What does the writer's sister think about the day?
o: She would like to do it again

l.intro: A woman tells a friend how she got engaged.

script.t: Viktor, I have news. Daulet and I got engaged on Saturday.
Congratulations! How did he propose?
Badly. He had planned everything for a restaurant, but he had booked the wrong day.
So what happened?
When we arrived, the restaurant had closed. He proposed in the car park.
That's romantic, in a way.
If he had checked the date, we would have had candles and music. But I said yes anyway.
Have you chosen a day for the wedding?
Next June. A small ceremony, about fifty guests, and the reception in my parents' garden.
And the honeymoon?
He wants to organise it himself. If he hadn't made that mistake on Saturday, I would have agreed.

ex.q: When did Aruzhan and Daulet get engaged?
Daulet proposed inside the restaurant.
What mistake did Daulet make?
Where will the reception be?

g.title: be, do and have: auxiliary and main verbs
g.rule:
These three verbs do two jobs.

main verbsI am a teacher. · I do my homework. · I have a flat.
auxiliariesI am working. · Do you like it? · I have finished.
emphasisI do like New York. · It did rain.
short answers and tagsYes, I have. · You're American, aren't you?

ex.q: ___ you ever been to the USA?
I ___ like the city, but it is expensive.
She lives in London, ___ she?

talk: What differences do you know between British and American English?
Would you like to live in the USA or the UK? Why or why not?

r.text:
I do speak English. I have studied it for ten years, and I have a certificate. So I didn't expect any problems when I moved from London to Chicago.

On my first day I asked a colleague where the lift was. She didn't understand until I pointed at it. "Oh, the elevator!" Then I told her that my flat was near the motorway, and she laughed. Americans have apartments and highways.

Lunch was worse. I ordered fish and chips and got a bag of crisps. I did complain, politely, and I did stand in the queue again, which is a "line" here.

My colleagues are kind about it. "You're British, aren't you?" they say. "Say 'trousers' again." I am not British, in fact. I am from Almaty, and I learned my English in London.

It is autumn now, or "fall". I am taking a holiday next month. I have decided to call it a vacation.

ex.q: Where did the writer move to?
The colleague understood the word "lift" immediately.
What did the writer get instead of chips?
Where is the writer from?

l.intro: A British visitor asks an American for directions.

script.t: Excuse me, is there a petrol station near here?
A gas station? Sure. Do you have a car?
I do, but it's two streets away. Can I walk there on the pavement?
On the sidewalk, yes. It's five minutes. You're British, aren't you?
I am. Is it that obvious?
A little. Go past the apartment building and take the elevator down to the lower street.
The lift. Right. And is there somewhere to buy crisps? I haven't eaten since breakfast.
Chips? There's a store next to the gas station. But there's usually a long line.
I don't mind a queue. We do love queuing at home.
I have heard that. Are you here on vacation?
On holiday, yes. And I did learn four new words today.

ex.q: What is the visitor looking for?
The visitor has a car.
What does the visitor want to buy?
What does the local say about the store?
o: There is usually a long line

g.title: Revision of verb forms
g.rule:
A quick map of the main verb forms.

presentI revise every day. · I'm revising now. · I've revised three topics.
pastI revised. · I was revising. · I had revised. · I used to revise.
futureI'm going to pass. · I'll help you. · I'm taking it tomorrow.
conditionals and passiveIf I pass, I'll celebrate. · The results will be sent.

ex.q: I ___ for this exam since March.
The results ___ next week.
If I had revised more, I ___ (pass).

talk: How do you prepare for an important exam?
Describe the best or worst exam you have ever taken.

r.text:
I am taking my final exam tomorrow at nine, and I have been revising for three weeks. I have made notes on every topic, and my friend has tested me twice.

I used to be terrible at exams. At school I once failed a history test because I was so nervous that I couldn't read the questions. I had revised for days, but when the invigilator said "Turn over your papers", my mind went empty. I had to retake it a month later.

This year I have changed my method. I stop revising at eight in the evening. I don't look at my notes in the morning. If the first question is hard, I will start with the multiple-choice section and write the essay afterwards.

The results will be sent to us in July. If I pass, I'll celebrate with my family. If I don't get a good mark, I'm going to try again in the autumn.

Now I am closing my books. It is five to eight.

ex.q: When is the exam?
The writer failed a history test at school.
What will the writer do if the first question is hard?
When does the writer stop revising?

l.intro: Two students meet after an exam.

script.t: Daniyar! How did it go?
I'm not sure. I was so nervous that I read the first question three times.
Me too. I had revised the wrong chapter, so the essay was a shock.
What did you write about?
Something about cities. I used to hate essays, but I think this one was fine.
The multiple-choice section was harder than last year's. I've never seen question twelve before.
I guessed that one. Did you see the invigilator take a phone from the boy at the back?
Yes. He was cheating. He'll have to retake the whole exam.
When are we getting the results?
They'll be sent by email in two weeks. If I pass, I'm going to sleep for a day.
If we both pass, I'll buy the pizza. Don't think about the marks now.

ex.q: How did Daniyar feel during the exam?
Malika had revised the right chapter.
Why did the invigilator take a phone?
How will they get the results?
